d4-brief-borrowed-brain.scenario: Solant Capital, a boutique SEC-registered investment adviser, wants to ship PortfolioSense, an assistant that drafts personalized investment recommendations for client meetings. Engineering lead Dan Okafor's team downloaded Kestrel-13B, an open-weights foundation model, and fine-tuned it for six weeks on Solant's internal research notes, prior client correspondence, and portfolio commentary going back to 2019. Kestrel-13B ships under a permissive base license, but Dan's team also pulled in a fine-tuning toolkit whose dependency chain carries a copyleft, share-alike clause neither engineering nor legal has reviewed. Dan wants to launch before the Q3 rebalancing cycle, three weeks away, and is treating the fine-tune as a minor customization of a model Solant never has to re-certify. Compliance officer Renata Voss has flagged that there is no AI bill of materials, no license review, no updated impact assessment, and no forecast of what happens if PortfolioSense's advice reaches a client Solant never intended it for. As a fiduciary, Solant answers to the SEC for every recommendation this tool produces. You are asked to write the governance position before engineering merges to the release branch.
d4-brief-borrowed-brain.fields[0].prompt: How does fine-tuning Kestrel-13B change Solant's liability and assurance posture compared to using it as-is?
d4-brief-borrowed-brain.fields[1].prompt: What does the license review of the fine-tuning toolkit's dependency chain need to check, and what is the single greatest long-term risk in it?
d4-brief-borrowed-brain.fields[2].prompt: What downstream or secondary-use harms should Solant forecast before shipping PortfolioSense, and by what method?
d4-brief-borrowed-brain.fields[3].prompt: What documentation and inventory must exist before Dan's team merges to the release branch?

d4-brief-silent-update.scenario: Larkspur Talent licenses ScreenWise, a hiring copilot built by vendor Aptivus AI, to score resumes and shortlist candidates for its client Marlowe Foods. The contract with Aptivus is silent on advance notice for model changes and gives Marlowe no audit rights over training data or evaluation reports. Three weeks ago, Aptivus pushed a model update, v4.2, to all customers with no notification and no changelog. On Monday, Marlowe's People Analytics lead, Priya Shah, ran the quarterly fairness check and found that the passthrough rate for female-coded resumes in engineering roles had fallen from 34% to 27.6% since the update landed — a gap under the company's 2% flat escalation trigger for average score drift, but one that lands squarely on a protected class. ScreenWise is still live and still screening today's applicants. General counsel has not yet been briefed, no public statement exists, and a labor-rights nonprofit has already emailed asking whether Marlowe is aware of "reports of bias" in its hiring tools. You are the governance lead. Priya wants a decision before end of day.
d4-brief-silent-update.fields[0].prompt: State your containment decision for ScreenWise and justify it against the alternative of leaving it live while you investigate.
d4-brief-silent-update.fields[1].prompt: Redesign the post-market monitoring plan so the next vendor-side model change is caught before candidates are harmed.
d4-brief-silent-update.fields[2].prompt: Draft the scope of your external communications response to the nonprofit's inquiry — what you disclose, and what you withhold.
d4-brief-silent-update.fields[3].prompt: Set the deactivation triggers and the restart criteria that must be met before ScreenWise goes back into production for Marlowe.

d4-case-bidder-questions.brief: A national tax authority is buying a tool that scores returns for audit selection, and it has hired an advisory firm to run the tender. Two bidders make the shortlist. The firm's questionnaire asks each for its error rates on past audits, a breakdown of which taxpayer populations its training records span, and a walkthrough of how scores are produced; the firm recommends the bidder with the lowest error rate, and the authority prepares to sign. Before signature, governance is asked to audit the tender itself: what the questionnaire covered, what it left open, and what still has to be settled before go-live.
d4-case-bidder-questions.steps[0].why: None of the three questionnaire items touches cybersecurity, resilience or vulnerability to attack — error rates cover validity, the scoring walkthrough covers explainability, and population coverage covers fairness/discrimination, but nothing in the request asks about the system's technical robustness or its exposure to unauthorized access, which matters even more given the sensitivity of the data involved.
d4-case-bidder-questions.steps[1].why: Asking how representative the training data is serves to catch models that perform unevenly across demographic groups before they are deployed, which makes it a fairness check. It is not tied to a single legal mandate, reliability is what the error-rate figures address, and explainability is what the scoring walkthrough was for.
d4-case-bidder-questions.steps[2].why: The AUP is the document that actually sets the terms of use — permitted purposes, prohibited uses, operational limits — which is exactly what's needed to govern ongoing operations. The privacy, security and code-of-conduct policies each cover a narrower slice (data handling, technical safeguards, internal ethics) but none defines what the tool may and may not be used for.
d4-case-bidder-questions.steps[3].why: An impact assessment asks whether deploying the tool at all is defensible for the people it affects — for a public audit-selection tool, that's the threshold question, and it has to be settled before a purely technical risk assessment (probability and severity of failure) can even be meaningful. They are genuinely different assessments, not two names for the same thing, and neither is 'only best practice' — both are expected, but impact comes first.
d4-case-bidder-questions.steps[4].why: A closed, proprietary system creates a long-term dependency — pricing, roadmap and portability are all in the vendor's hands, and switching later gets harder the longer the authority stays. Biased output is a real risk but applies just as much to the open alternative, integration problems are a near-term engineering fix rather than a strategic one, and subscription cost is a budgeting question, not what limits future choices.

d4-case-fraud-rfp.brief: Harrowby Savings Bank, a regional lender, is buying a cloud-hosted AI service from an American software vendor to flag suspicious card payments as they happen. The vendor's draft contract keeps all model IP with the vendor, forbids the bank from changing or retraining the model, offers performance reporting at intervals, and disclaims liability for both missed fraud and wrongly blocked payments. Before anything is signed, procurement wants governance to mark up the agreement and confirm that Harrowby will have adequate oversight, IP protection and visibility into open-source risk.
d4-case-fraud-rfp.steps[0].why: Errors in fraud screening land on customers directly: missed fraud lets money leave an account, and a wrongly blocked payment stops a genuine purchase. If the vendor accepts no liability for either, Harrowby carries every financial, regulatory and reputational consequence alone and has nothing in the contract to fall back on. Vendor IP ownership and the retraining ban restrict flexibility without creating that exposure, and periodic performance reports add transparency rather than risk.
d4-case-fraud-rfp.steps[1].why: Oversight and auditability depend on the bank actually being able to see into the system — its data, documentation and model internals — not on who is liable, who owns the outputs, or who ships upgrades; those matter for different disputes, not for whether the bank can audit and evaluate the system it's running.
d4-case-fraud-rfp.steps[2].why: Indemnification is the mechanism that shifts an infringement claim's legal costs and damages onto the vendor. Insurance only pays out if the vendor's carrier honors the policy — it doesn't obligate the vendor to defend the bank; a performance warranty covers whether the tool works, not who owns the underlying IP; and a privacy notice governs personal-data use, not infringement risk.
d4-case-fraud-rfp.steps[3].why: Jurisdictional scope is one of the most common carve-outs in SaaS indemnification: the vendor never assessed or priced its exposure in a country it didn't agree to cover, so deploying there voids the protection precisely when the bank needs it most. Indemnification isn't unlimited, doesn't scale with exposure, and it's a contract term — not something a regulator inherits.
d4-case-fraud-rfp.steps[4].why: AGPL is the copyleft license that reaches even network-accessible use: anyone interacting with the service over a network can demand the corresponding source, which pulls in whatever proprietary code the bank wrapped around it. Missed accuracy benchmarks, API misuse and a slide into the public domain are all real vendor risks, but none is what an unreviewed AGPL dependency actually triggers.

d4-case-ours-alone.brief: A regional bank's data-science group has spent the past year building an in-house fraud-scoring model instead of buying one, training it entirely on the bank's own transaction history and validating it internally. The model launches this quarter. The board's risk committee wants to understand, before sign-off, how governing a proprietary build differs from governing a vendor tool — and what specifically the bank now owns that it wouldn't own with a bought system.
d4-case-ours-alone.steps[0].why: Liability is the one risk that doesn't go away with good behavior: a proprietary model can still cause harm through edge cases or unforeseen conditions after every current standard has been met, and there's no vendor to share the resulting damages, lawsuits or reputational fallout with. Cost, compliance burden and obsolescence are all manageable through budgeting and monitoring; liability persists regardless.
d4-case-ours-alone.steps[1].why: With no vendor's documentation to point to, the bank's own paper trail — training data, testing, model cards, decision logs — is the only evidence it has for compliance and defense. There's no vendor to negotiate a cap with, no second provider to share blame with, and no external approval to lean on; the obligation is squarely the bank's own record-keeping.
d4-case-ours-alone.steps[2].why: Bias is a risk in every model regardless of who built it — a bought system needs the same fairness testing a homegrown one does. Sourcing your own training data, running your own conformity assessment, and carrying your own compute costs, by contrast, are burdens a vendor purchase would have absorbed or shared.
d4-case-ours-alone.steps[3].why: A vendor disclaimer shifts the paperwork, not the deployer's underlying duty of due diligence — governance holds the organization that put the tool into production accountable for validating it, disclaimer or not. The vendor and the employee share some blame at most, and blaming the customer isn't a defense at all; the primary duty sits with the deployer.
d4-case-ours-alone.steps[4].why: Standard tech E&O wording predates algorithmic decisioning and routinely excludes exactly the claims an AI system generates, so that's the specific gap a proprietary-model review has to close — not the size of the cap, physical-outage terms, or pricing, which are generic policy mechanics unrelated to what makes this system's risk different.
